rv.q: The actress is astonishing as a widow named Marjorie in the superb revival of Jordan Harrison’s haunting science-fiction drama that opened Monday night.
Sometimes it’s the harmonic adventurousness I treasure, sometimes the way she always finds the musical equivalent of the mot juste.

The conclusion we take away from the haunting final scene of Mr. Harrison’s probing drama is that if technology arrives at creating near-perfect replicas of people, they will be shinier, more placid and ultimately hollow versions of human beings.

In an unprepossessing way, the show evokes the possibility of a post-human future in which machines go on forever, asking the same questions over and over, or perhaps answering them on their own and moving on … but to what?
But it does, for a moment, penetrate the fog.
There will be only polite recalibration.
With its novelty gone, Marjorie Prime must rely more firmly on its internal mechanics, which can be creaky.
Nixon turns on a dime when her character realizes, as I think many of us have or will, that this brave new world of now is short on both guardrails and moral principles.
Marjorie Prime is very much a play for our times.
Her Marjories (real and Prime) are measured, funny, vulnerable, and tough—two colorful, intriguing human portraits.
In Prime, an ironic version of a family drama, the entire cast seems entirely at home.
Plays hardly come as astutely, or productions as perceptive as this – and rarely anyone as brilliantly as Squibb.
In a culture increasingly eager to outsource discomfort, this quiet, unsettling play asks what we lose when we do—and whether comfort, once commodified, can ever truly be returned.
A quietly persuasive tale of well-intentioned hubris, Marjorie Prime is the tragedy of right now.
Regardless, these scenes between Squibb (in kinder and gentler mode) and Nixon (suitably lost) are among the show's best.
Harrison's spare, gently gripping script is a model of eloquent economy as the characters grapple with grief and what it means to truly love and remember someone.
There is no replacement for the power of human love and connection.
An unusually gentle piece, it nevertheless sends a chill up one's spine.

Certainly that is something to ponder during the play's final scene, which may be intended as a grace note of irony but which, in retrospect, does not seem ironic at all as we wade into the unknown waters of a brave new world.
This play may finally be hitting too close to home.
There is still much in the play that I find clever and thought-provoking.
This remarkable revival, once again directed by Anne Kauffman, feels so much more potent.
When it was all over, I much preferred watching the actors impersonate machines in Harrison’s sci-fi tale than watching them impersonate human beings.

For that reason, Marjorie Prime has its own well-deserved chance at immortality, as a melancholic meditation on how there wasn’t really a time when humans could be forgotten, because nobody is ever truly known.
June Squibb and a superb company turn Marjorie Prime into an acting masterclass about mortality, memory, and why we love. Brian
Marjorie Prime is the best, tightest, most well written, thought provoking, absolutely brilliant 90 minutes that I’ve seen on Broadway in a very long time.
“Marjorie Prime” ranks among the finest productions of the season.

cn.t: Critics praise this timely AI drama as quietly devastating and emotionally precise, with June Squibb's performance earning raves. Some find it feels dated or overly familiar a decade after its premiere.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.

vr.q: June Squibb is absolutely luminous. She's so funny and vulnerable and commands the stage.
Go check out Marjorie Prime. I really think it's worth it to see these wonderful actors in this thoughtprovoking play.
